messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Vignette:
Maren Kowalski is a 31-year-old Polish-American paramedic who presented for psychological assessment following a prolonged period of distress she described, with some reluctance, as "finally getting bad enough that I can't pretend it isn't there." Divorced eighteen months ago, she lives alone in a mid-sized Midwestern city and works rotating shifts with a municipal emergency medical service. She has no prior psychiatric history.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Maren was off-duty and alone when she was stopped by two police officers near her apartment building following a noise complaint in the area. What began as a routine interaction escalated rapidly. One of the officers, without warning, grabbed her by the arm and forced her against the wall of the building. She described the physical sensation of her cheek against cold brick, the officer's weight pressing into her back, and a second officer standing close, blocking any exit. She was not formally arrested, and the encounter ended within minutes — but not before she experienced what she understood, even in the moment, to be a complete loss of control over her own body and safety. She drove home, showered, and did not tell anyone for weeks.

In the months that followed, Maren noticed changes she initially attributed to work stress. She began to feel nauseated before shifts, particularly on days she knew might bring her into contact with police at accident scenes or emergency calls — a routine and unavoidable feature of her job. The nausea became its own signal, arriving before she had consciously registered any threat, and she began to dread it as much as the situations that preceded it. At work, she found herself repositioning constantly — choosing where to stand in a room, angling herself toward exits, cataloguing who was present and where. Colleagues noticed she had stopped sitting with her back to the door in the break room, but she offered no explanation.

When a supervising officer from a different agency attended a multi-agency incident and placed a hand on her shoulder to redirect her attention, Maren startled so visibly that the officer stepped back in alarm. She left the scene early, citing equipment failure. She had come to believe that any unexpected physical contact carried within it the possibility of what had happened before — that the body, once handled that way, could be handled that way again at any moment. This belief had become so entrenched that even a colleague reaching past her in the ambulance could make her flinch and go rigid.

Maren has systematically altered her routes, her routines, and her social life to minimise contact with anyone in uniform or in a position of institutional authority. She declined a promotion that would have required more coordination with law enforcement. She stopped attending a weekly dinner with friends after one of them began dating a police officer and occasionally brought him along. She has never allowed herself to express anger about what happened — she described this with a kind of flat precision, saying she was afraid of what it would mean if she let herself feel how angry she was, as though the anger itself were dangerous. Instead, she described a persistent internal flatness punctuated by sudden, overwhelming moments she could not fully account for.

When asked to describe the incident in detail during her intake session, Maren stopped several times mid-sentence, lost the thread of what she was saying, and eventually said she could not be certain of the order in which things had happened. She knew the broad shape of it but could not place the pieces sequentially with any confidence. More troubling to her was the quality of the memories when they did surface — she was certain, in those moments, that it was not over. It did not feel like remembering. It felt like it was still happening.

What finally brought her to seek help was a shift last month in which she froze at a scene while a police officer approached her from behind. Her partner had to step in. Maren sat in the ambulance afterward and understood, for the first time, that this was no longer something she could manage by rearranging her world around it. She came to the first session saying she did not want to talk about it, but that she needed, somehow, to make it feel finished.
